lessonTitle: Team Roles and Dynamics: Stages, RACI and Resolving Conflict

blocks.text: Six weeks into a student formula-car project the chassis sub-team has produced three incompatible suspension layouts, two members are no longer speaking, and the team leader is about to blame 'personality clashes'. In fact the team is behaving in a predictable, well-studied way. Recognising the pattern lets a leader act on causes, such as unclear roles and unresolved disagreement, rather than on personalities.

blocks.markdown: Engineering is done in teams, and teams change over time. **Tuckman's model** describes four stages that most new teams pass through: **forming**, **storming**, **norming** and **performing**, with a fifth stage, **adjourning**, when the project ends. Progress is not guaranteed: teams can stall in storming, or revert when membership or goals change.

rows: Members meet, are polite, and depend on the leader
Uncertainty about goals and roles; low trust
Clarify purpose, roles and ground rules
Competing ideas and power struggles surface
Conflict over methods, leadership and workload
Make decisions explicit; use evidence; manage disagreement
Norms and working methods are agreed
The team works effectively and autonomously
The project ends and the team disbands
blocks.caption: Tuckman's stages of team development.

blocks.title: Conflict is normal, not a failure
blocks.text: Storming is a necessary stage in which differences of approach are tested. It becomes destructive only if it is ignored, personalised or never resolved.

blocks.markdown: Clear roles prevent a large share of conflict. A **responsibility assignment (RACI) matrix** lists tasks (rows) against people (columns) and marks each cell with one of four letters. **R**esponsible: does the work. **A**ccountable: owns the outcome and approves it, with the final say. **C**onsulted: gives input before decisions (two-way). **I**nformed: told of the outcome (one-way).

blocks.title: Rules for a valid RACI matrix
blocks.text: Every task has exactly one A, at least one R (the A may also be the R), and no blank rows. Too many C and I entries slow decisions. Check that no person is over-loaded.

blocks.caption: Example RACI matrix for four tasks and four people.

blocks.title: Checking and using a RACI matrix
blocks.prompt: Using the table above, verify that the matrix is valid and say who should approve the FEA of the wishbone and who should be consulted.

steps.text: Count A per row: suspension geometry has one A (Sam); FEA has one (Jonas, combined with R); procurement one (Mei); test plan one (Sam). Every row has exactly one A.
Check R: every row has at least one R (Priya, Jonas, Mei and Sam respectively).
FEA of wishbone: Jonas is accountable and responsible, so he approves the result; Priya is consulted before decisions, and Sam and Mei are informed afterwards.
Check load: Sam is A on two tasks and R on one; the matrix is valid, but Sam's workload should be reviewed.

blocks.answer: The matrix is valid. Jonas approves the FEA; Priya is consulted.

blocks.markdown: **Resolving conflict** starts by understanding the facts, not by deciding who is right. Useful principles are to separate the people from the problem, focus on **interests** (what each person needs) rather than **positions** (what each demands), and rely on **evidence** such as task logs, meeting minutes and test data. The Thomas-Kilmann model describes five conflict-handling modes: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating; collaborating is most suitable when the issue is important and a good outcome needs both parties' input.

blocks.title: Evidence-based conflict resolution
blocks.prompt: In a four-person team, Mei complains that Alex 'never does any work'. Alex says he is 'doing his share'. Hours logged over the last month are Priya 52, Jonas 40, Mei 36 and Alex 12. Analyse the evidence and propose an approach.

steps.text: Interpret carefully: the log supports Mei's concern, but ask why. Alex may have been assigned tasks that were blocked, been unclear about his role, or been unwell, and hours do not measure output.

Approach: hold a private conversation with Alex to understand his view, then a facilitated team meeting that reviews the log and the RACI, agree specific tasks and deadlines for Alex, and review in two weeks.

blocks.answer: The data show an imbalance (8.6% of hours against a 25% equal share), but the cause should be understood before any action; the resolution is a clear, evidence-based plan for redistributing tasks.

blocks.title: Avoid the common mistakes
blocks.text: Do not decide on hearsay; do not argue about personalities; do not let a conflict fester because it is uncomfortable; and do not let the loudest voice settle technical questions without evidence.

points: Teams typically move through forming, storming, norming and performing, with adjourning at the end, and each stage has typical issues and leader actions.
A RACI matrix assigns Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed roles; a valid matrix has exactly one A per task and at least one R.
Conflicts are resolved by focusing on interests and on evidence such as logs, minutes and data, leading to a specific plan with a review.

questions.stem: A newly formed design team is meeting for the first time. Members are courteous but hesitant, unsure who decides what, and wait for the leader to give instructions. Which stage of development is this?

options.text: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: politeness, dependence on the leader and uncertainty about roles are typical of forming.
distractorRationale.b: Storming involves open conflict and challenge.
distractorRationale.d: Performing is a mature, autonomous stage.

questions.explanation: In forming, members are cautious and dependent on the leader. The leader's main task is to clarify purpose, roles and ground rules.

questions.stem: Three months into a robotics project, two sub-teams argue persistently over which control architecture to use, and members challenge the team leader's decisions. What is the appropriate interpretation and response?

options.text: The team has failed and should be disbanded
It is typical storming; the leader should make the decision process explicit and base it on evidence
The team is in performing and should be left alone
The leader should avoid the conflict until it disappears

questions.correctOptionText: It is typical storming; the leader should make the decision process explicit and base it on evidence

distractorRationale.a: Conflict is expected and can be productive.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: storming is a normal stage and is managed by clarifying decisions and using evidence.
distractorRationale.c: Performing teams work cooperatively with agreed methods.

questions.explanation: Storming reflects the testing of ideas and leadership. A clear decision process supported by evidence keeps it constructive and helps the team to move on to norming.

questions.stem: A RACI matrix for a test programme shows two people marked 'A' for the task 'Approve test report'. What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem
There should be exactly one accountable person per task, so accountability is unclear
Nobody is responsible for doing the work
The task needs more people informed

questions.correctOptionText: There should be exactly one accountable person per task, so accountability is unclear

distractorRationale.a: It breaks the rule that each task has a single owner.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: one A per task ensures a single point of accountability.
distractorRationale.c: The matrix does not say anything about R in this case.
distractorRationale.d: I entries are not the issue.

questions.explanation: Accountability means owning the outcome and having the final say. Two accountable people create ambiguity over who decides and who answers for the result.

questions.stem: In a RACI matrix, what is the difference between Responsible and Accountable?

options.text: Responsible does the work; Accountable owns the outcome and approves it
They mean the same thing
Responsible approves; Accountable is only informed
Accountable does the work; Responsible is only consulted

questions.correctOptionText: Responsible does the work; Accountable owns the outcome and approves it

distractorRationale.a: Correct: R performs the task, A has ownership and sign-off.
distractorRationale.b: They are distinct roles, though one person may hold both.

questions.explanation: The responsible person carries out the work, while the accountable person owns the result and has final approval. One person may be both for a small task, but each task has just one accountable person.

questions.stem: A team member is Responsible for three tasks needing 14 h, 22 h and 9 h of work. They can commit 6 h per week for 6 weeks. What is their workload as a percentage of available time?
questions.explanation: Total assigned work is 14 + 22 + 9 = 45 h and available time is 6 x 6 = 36 h. The workload is 45/36 = 1.25, i.e. 125%, which means they are over-allocated and the matrix should be rebalanced.

questions.stem: A five-person team logs 46, 38, 30, 22 and 14 hours of work in a month. What percentage of the total hours was contributed by the member who logged 14 hours? Give the answer to one decimal place in percent.
questions.explanation: Total hours are 46 + 38 + 30 + 22 + 14 = 150. The share is 14/150 = 0.0933, i.e. 9.3%, compared with 20% for an equal share. Such data are evidence to discuss, not proof of fault.

questions.stem: Two team members disagree about whose task is late. What is the best first step towards an evidence-based resolution?

options.text: Side with the more senior member
Collect the facts, such as the schedule, task log and meeting minutes, and hear each person's view separately
Ask the entire team to vote
Ignore the dispute in the hope it fades

questions.correctOptionText: Collect the facts, such as the schedule, task log and meeting minutes, and hear each person's view separately

distractorRationale.b: Correct: establishing the facts and hearing each person leads to a fair resolution.
distractorRationale.c: A vote on facts is not a substitute for evidence.

questions.explanation: Evidence-based resolution begins by gathering objective information and listening to each party. Only then can the leader agree actions that address the actual cause.

questions.stem: Avoiding a conflict is the best strategy for a team leader because disagreements usually resolve themselves.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Avoided conflicts tend to persist or escalate. Resolution needs the facts, an understanding of each party's interests and agreed actions, though avoiding can be a sensible short-term choice for a trivial issue.

questions.stem: A team of five students designs and builds an electric go-kart over two semesters. Describe the four main stages of team development the team is likely to pass through, giving a typical issue at each stage and an action the team leader should take.
markingGuide: Forming: uncertainty and politeness; clarify goals, roles and ground rules
Storming: conflict over methods and leadership; manage disagreement with evidence and explicit decisions
Norming: agreeing working methods and norms; reinforce processes and watch for groupthink
Performing: effective, autonomous work; delegate and maintain standards
Mentions adjourning or that stages may recur when circumstances change
Examples relate to the go-kart context
questions.explanation: The marker credits correct stage names and a distinct issue and leader action for each. Examples tied to the project show understanding rather than recall.

questions.stem: A four-person team (Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev) has four tasks: CAD of chassis, structural FEA, procurement of motors, and test plan. Draw up a RACI matrix (list it in text), justify your allocation, and check it against the rules for a valid matrix.
markingGuide: Lists tasks against the four members with R, A, C and I
Each task has exactly one A
Each task has at least one R
Allocation is justified (skills, workload balance, avoids over-loading one person)
Consulted and informed roles are sensible and not excessive
Checks the matrix against the rules and the workload
questions.explanation: The marker checks the matrix for exactly one A per task and at least one R, and credits sensible justification of who is consulted or informed. Over-loading one person or leaving a row without an owner loses marks.
